schools.summary: Gill makes the 'tabernacle' the church of God on earth, not Christ's humanity nor heaven, since 'abide' means to sojourn or lodge as in an inn and will not suit a fixed, immovable state; Calvin lifts it to the covenant condition that God's people show themselves holy by an upright life, hypocrites who occupy the temple vainly pretending.

Henry hears 'who shall abide' as 'who shall go to heaven' (not by name but by description), the tabernacle the church militant and the holy hill the church triumphant; Spurgeon insists that on the ground of law no mere man can dwell with God, only through the Advocate whose righteousness endures for ever.

Clarke presses the Hebrew: mi yagur ('sojourn/lodge') marks the migratory tabernacle, type of the militant church with no continuing city, and mi yiscon ('dwell') the fixed temple, type of the rest that remains.

Ellicott takes the two terms as synonyms, the verse asking what makes a true citizen of God's kingdom; Keil and Delitzsch read it as the answer to the previous psalm's righteous generation, beside Ps. 24 and the Ark's removal, the bare 'holy mountain' inclining them to the Absalom exile.

Augustine reads the tabernacle as a thing of war (soldiers are tent-fellows) fitting the season we war with the devil, and the holy mountain as the eternal rest, the supereminence of Christ's love in life everlasting.

debates.question: Do 'tabernacle' and 'holy hill' mark two distinct states or one abode in synonymous parallelism?

sides.position: two states — the church militant (sojourn) and the church triumphant or heaven (dwell)
synonymous parallelism for the one church/abode of God on earth

outliers.note: Reads the whole question allegorically — the tabernacle a soldier's war-tent for our combat with the devil, the holy mountain the eternal love of Christ — lifting the historical David into the temporal Dispensation of the Incarnation.

themes: who shall abide in thy tabernacle

schools.summary: Gill guards 'uprightly'/'perfectly' against a false rigour: not to be without sin, but not chargeable with a notorious crime — perfection here is sincerity, an Israelite indeed in whom is no guile.

Keil and Delitzsch note the answer worked out in three tristichs, the perfect tenses carrying the force of abstract presents (tried, habitual qualities); Ellicott renders the line 'perfect rectitude' (Prov. 28:18) and takes truth in the heart as both thought and spoken.

Clarke reads holech tamim (God set before his eyes, his word the rule) and poel tsedek (rendering all their dues), heart, tongue, and hand in unison; Wesley: serving God and neighbour in truth and constantly, words agreeing with the heart.

Henry reads a man sincere in religion, walking per the covenant with Abraham (Gen. 17:1), an Israelite without guile (John 1:47) whose prayers come not from feigned lips; Spurgeon takes it as an outward character with faith the hidden root, the upright man erect, God's house a hive for workers not a nest for drones.

Gill draws 'backbiteth' from the root for 'foot' — a tale-bearer going house to house (a kindred word means spies), prying into families' secrets and divulging them, unfit for the society of the saints.

Clarke: 'he foots not upon his tongue,' the backbiter a knave, coward, and dog; 'reproach' (cherpah) a stripping bare, as winter (choreph) strips the fields, and the good man 'will not bear it' onward. Wesley: he neither raises nor spreads a reproach, nor believes it without sufficient reason.

Ellicott: 'footed it on his tongue' (house-to-house tittle-tattle, 1 Tim. 5:13); 'reproach' from the stripping of trees of autumn fruit; two Hebrew words for 'neighbour'; the marginal 'receiveth/endureth' quite against the context.

Henry: does hurt to no man and is tender of his neighbour's good name, frowning on a backbiting tongue (Prov. 25:23), neither raising nor receiving a reproach but disproving it or letting it die with him, his charity covering a multitude of sins.

debates.question: Does 'taketh up a reproach' mean to carry a slander onward, or to receive and believe it?

sides.position: to raise or carry a reproach onward (and refuse to), the marginal 'receiveth/endureth' set aside
reaching also to the receiving or too-ready believing of a reproach

schools.summary: Ellicott owns the first clause obscure but holds the AV right — the contemptible are contemned, the God-fearing honoured — against reading 'despised in his own eyes'; notes the LXX 'to his neighbour' for 'to his own hurt.'

Gill: the vile person despised as an abomination to God (Haman by Mordecai, Ahab by Elisha), yet allows the clause may be rendered of a good man 'despised in his own eyes' (Targum, Aben Ezra, Kimchi), the humble sense, though he thinks the former better countenanced.

Clarke: nimas the reprobate, nibzeh loathsome as leprosy, contempt pointed at vice; relays Aben Ezra's 'contemptible in his own eyes' (Luke 17:10) but judges the next clause disproves it; the bare word binds as an oath; the Chaldee reads 'sweareth to afflict himself.' Wesley: honours the God-fearing though mean and differing in lesser opinions; a promissory oath kept to his own damage.
Henry marvels at the bond: even wise men may swear to their own hurt unawares, yet an oath is sacred and must be kept at a loss rather than played fast and loose with.

debates.question: Does the first clause mean 'a vile person is contemned' or 'he is despised in his own eyes' (self-abasement)?

sides.position: the wicked are held in contempt while the God-fearing are honoured
the good man is contemptible in his own eyes, an expression of humility

debates.question: Does the oath-clause read 'sweareth to his own hurt,' 'to afflict himself,' or 'to his neighbour'?

sides.position: 'to his own hurt/damage' — the received reading
'to afflict himself' (the Chaldee), of one vowing to keep his body under
'to his neighbour' (the Septuagint, by transposing the letters)

themes: he honoureth them that fear the LORD
sweareth to his own hurt and changeth not

schools.summary: Gill condemns the biting, exorbitant usury that devours the poor, but holds moderate interest by law lawful as rent on houses and land; the design is to forbid oppression, and the covetous are unfit for church communion.

Ellicott: usury allowed with foreigners (Deut. 23:20), the laws made to protect the poor, not because interest is wrong in itself (Exod. 22:25; Lev. 25:36); the sin here, joined to bribery, is limited to unjust 'biting' usury, honest capital for trade not averse (the parable of the talents).

Clarke: usury is unlawful interest wrung from a distressed neighbour, neshech 'to bite as a serpent'; 'reward against the innocent' the lawyer's fee to plead against the poor. Wesley keeps the plainest line — usury as lending contrary to God's law, 'reward' a bribe for a bad cause, 'never moved' to abide with God here and for ever hereafter.
Henry: he will not increase his estate by extortion or bribery; 'he that doeth these things shall never be moved,' like Zion-hill built on a rock (Ps. 125:1), kept safe by sufficient grace.

debates.question: Does the psalm forbid all lending at interest, or only the 'biting' usury that preys on the poor?

sides.position: only oppressive, biting usury of the poor is condemned; honest, moderate interest is lawful
usury kept as a plain prohibition, lending contrary to God's law

themes: putteth not out his money to usury
